newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish bull run continues despite EMU jitters.
newsitem.headline: Spanish bull run continues despite EMU jitters.

text.p: The bull run in Spanish markets has remained intact despite fears that a new coalition in France could bring a watered-down version of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) convergence requirements.
Madrid stocks and bonds outpaced sister markets in Europe on Monday and Tuesday, supported by domestic investment trust demand and economic fundamentals.
Dealers said that as long as EMU happened on time, Spain should profit from it, even if the deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) criteria ratio was changed.
"The EMU project is not badly affected (by the Socialist win in the first round of the French election)," Societe Generale brokerage said in a note to clients on Tuesday..
"A softer policy seems to be the most likely outcome (and) this suggests higher yields of so-called core countries, and maybe a larger union, with a lower spread for peripheral markets."
On Tuesday afternoon the most liquid share index Ibex-35 gained 1.7 percent to 6,693.4, while the general index was 1.5 percent higher at a record high of 579.31, with dealers expecting more highs.
"There is more scope for stocks to rise," said Javier Requena, chief economist at Benito y Monjardin in Madrid.
The long bond future gained 37 basis points at 115.44, with the 10-year spread at 67 basis points, not far from its record low of 64 points hit past Wednesday.
Although the possibility of higher yields in core countries was still remote, analysts said that the outlook particularly favoured stocks.

"If the left wing should win in France (in the second round on June 1) that could delay their privatisation programme, while we do not have such doubts here in Spain," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
For the new French government the first test will be Thomson-Csf with a winner expected to be chosen for its privatisation before the end of June, but a centre-left coalition could abort the deal.
In Spain, after having already successfully concluded two privatisations in Telefonica and Repsol, upcoming offers include Endesa, Retevision and Argentaria before the end of this year.
Tabacalera and Aldeasa are also in the pipeline.
This has raised the impression foreign investors could have unwound positions in France, switching money into Spain, but traders said no big movements were seen.
"It something we haven't seen. We still think international investors are very quiet here. Facing a domestically driven rally, they are waiting," said Nick Smith, trader at BZW in Madrid.
"The stock market rise in the last few months had a very high domestic component," said a dealer working with an investment trust.
"We are seeing a very high amount of net inflow, which we are investing in stocks" he added. "And sometimes foreigners are selling".
